- **T-033 — the pin is a constant, not an absence, and that is the whole point of the determinism requirement.** New **§3.4.1**: `BuildPhase.seedIsAuthoritative = true` short-circuits `PlaceCatalog.load()` to the bundled seed with no fetch attempted. Deliberately a **runtime constant, not `#if`** — both branches stay compiled, type-checked and greppable, so the live path can be reviewed in Phase 1 and the Phase-2 flip is one boolean in one file. Deliberately **not** "there's no plist, so it falls through": that is machine-dependent, holds on a machine that never had credentials and silently stops holding on one that does — which is exactly the accidental-pass `product` asked to rule out.
- **The determinism requirement is three pass/fail assertions, not a behavioural note.** In `PlaceCatalogTests`: (1) `source == .seed` after `load()`; (2) **zero** fetch attempts, proven by a `PlacesFetching` spy that fails the test if called at all; (3) assertion 1 **still holds with a populated `SupabaseConfig.plist` present**, supplied by the test — the assertion that distinguishes a pin from a fall-through, and the one that fails if someone later removes the constant as dead code. Assertion 2 needed a seam, so §3.4.1 adds `PlaceCatalog.init(api:cache:)` with protocol defaults — **the shipped `DensityStore.init(api:cache:now:)` idiom, read from the source, not a new pattern.** This is the only contract change in §4 this pass makes.
- **The built-but-unexercised gap is named up front, in two places.** New lead-in to **§4.3** and a new **§7** bullet: the `GET`, the `hoodID`-stamping decoder, the two live-only boundary rules, `PlacesCache`'s disk round trip, **and** the `.live`/`.cache`/`.unavailable` half of §4.8's error-vs-empty distinction (derived from `source`, which can only read `.seed` in Phase 1) all ship built and never run against a server. Phase-1 acceptance covers PRD reqs 1–7 against the fixture and covers none of that. Stated as T-031's "heat never observed live" shape explicitly, since that one had to be retroactively re-read as intentional at acceptance — naming it now is the entire point.
- **Fixture spec'd as two files with pass/fail floors, and the emitter conflict across phases reconciled.** §3.4.1 carries `product`'s floors verbatim in substance (real Tel Aviv names, both categories, coordinates inside the placeholder rectangle each `hood_id` names, ≥8 places / ≥2 Hoods, one Hood with zero places, one with no blurb, provisional declared in-file) with the numeric floors kept labelled **[ASSUMPTION]** as product's own judgment, not a founder threshold. - **Agree with `ios-developer`'s `isDepth1Presented`/`isDepth2Presented` finding** (§4.1 doesn't declare the two-way `Binding<Bool>` accessors §4.2's code uses, and a sheet swipe-dismiss needs the setter to route to `closeHood()`/`closePlace()` or the router desyncs from the screen) — independently verified against §4.1/§4.2's actual text, real and worth folding into §4.1 before C5, not blocking.
- **New finding 1 (should-fix, not blocking): the Hood button's z-order/visibility relationship to T-032's nav-surface presentation is unspecified in both TRDs, and it changes whether §4.2's cross-task rule is reachable.** Read `time-slider/TRD.md` §2.3's chrome table directly: while a nav-row surface (e.g. the heat modal) is presented, T-032 puts the scrim at z1 (blocks map taps — so a pin/polygon tap can never open a Hood sheet while a nav surface is up) and explicitly hides+disables hit-testing on "bucket-2 chrome" (`NearMeButton`+`SettingsHint`) at z2, while `MapNavRow` itself stays at z4, always visible and hit-testable. T-033's `HoodButton` (§4.7, D6) is built "to the existing `NearMeButton` chrome idiom... same bottom band" but T-032's z-order table was written without knowing `HoodButton` exists, and T-033's TRD never states which bucket it falls into. Two readings are both defensible and produce different behaviour: if `HoodButton` inherits `NearMeButton`'s bucket-2 treatment (hidden while a nav surface is presented), then §4.2's cross-task rule ("opening a Hood sheet or place modal from the map closes any open nav-row modal first") has **no reachable trigger left** — map taps are already blocked by the scrim, and the Hood button would be hidden too — making the rule dead code as currently scoped. If `HoodButton` is instead exempt like `MapNavRow` (always visible/hit-testable), the rule is real and necessary, and whichever task builds second must wire it exactly as both TRDs already flag. This needs one sentence in `HoodButton`'s spec (§4.7) or T-032's chrome table before C10 is built — cheap, not a redesign, and doesn't block `trd-review` clearing.
- **New finding 2 (should-fix, not blocking): `Place.hoodID`'s population path for the live fetch isn't stated.** §4.3's embedded `GET` shape is `hoods?select=id,blurb,places(id,name,category,latitude,longitude)` — no `hood_id` key appears per place row, because it's structurally implied by nesting under each Hood. But `Place` (§3.2) requires a `hoodID: String` field, and §4.3's boundary-validation table treats "`hood_id` not present in the bundled Hood catalog" as a condition to check against already-parsed `Place` values. Nothing in §3.2/§4.3/§4.4 states that `PlacesAPI`'s decoder must stamp `hoodID` from the enclosing Hood's `id` while walking the embedded response — a different decode path than the flat bundled seed (§3.4), where `hood_id` is presumably a literal column per row. ### 2026-07-31 — security-auditor — T-040/PAS-17 + T-042/PAS-19 systemic security sweep: PASS, no blocking findings

- **Scope:** the systemic sweep recommended (three times independently — `developer`, `code-reviewer`, `ios-developer`) across `hood-dataset/TRD.md` (T-040, `PAS-17`, migration `003_hood_attributes.sql` + `006_hoods_tel_aviv_data.sql`) and `places-dataset/TRD.md` (T-042, `PAS-19`, migration `004_places.sql`) before Aviran applies either — the check T-043's own `trd-review` already got and these two hadn't. Read both TRDs in full, `database/migrations/001_hoods_and_density.sql` and `002_synthetic_density_generator.sql` in full as the established pattern, `database/README.md`, and `database/scripts/export_hoods_geojson.py` (the only script that exists on disk today — `validate_dataset.py`/`build_hoods.py`/`export_places.py` are all still unwritten, matching both TRDs' own "not built yet" framing). Confirmed via `ls database/migrations/` that only `001`/`002` exist — neither `003`, `004`, nor `006` has been written, so this is a pre-build TRD-level review of SQL that will be generated, not a diff of applied code.
- **Verdict: PASS on both.** No Critical/High findings on either TRD. Nothing here blocks `build`.
- **The specific bug class named in the dispatch (unrevoked `security definer` — migration `002`'s `generate_synthetic_density()` and T-043's `hood_for_point()`/`reattribute_events()`) does not recur.** Grepped both TRDs' full SQL bodies: T-040's `003_hood_attributes.sql` is three `alter table add column if not exists` statements, no function. T-040's `006_hoods_tel_aviv_data.sql` is a generated `insert ... on conflict do update` plus a scoped `delete`, no function. T-042's `004_places.sql` is two `create table`, two `enable row level security` + one `select` policy each, one index — no function. **Neither task defines any PL/pgSQL or SQL function, `security definer` or otherwise** — there is nothing for PostgREST to auto-expose as an RPC endpoint in either migration. The bug class requires a function to exist first; it doesn't here. Confirmed this isn't a documentation gap either — `place_type`/`keywords`/geometry validation all happens in the offline Python validator (`validate_dataset.py`), explicitly *not* in Postgres (T-042 §4.1 clause 3: "There is no PostGIS on this project... a DB-level containment constraint would mean adding a spatial extension" — the architecture itself keeps logic out of the database, which is what keeps this bug class from having anywhere to land).
- **RLS — both new tables and both column sets match `001`'s already-accepted pattern exactly, checked against the actual SQL text, not the TRD's prose summary of it:** `places` and `place_types` (T-042 §3.3) get `enable row level security` + one `for select to anon, authenticated using (true)` policy each, **no insert/update/delete policy anywhere** — absence-is-denial, identical shape to `hoods_public_read`/`hood_density_public_read` in `001`. `hoods`' three new columns (T-040 §3.1: `blurb`, `is_tourist_trap`, `designated_for_progression`) get no new RLS statement at all, which is correct, not an oversight — RLS is row-scoped in Postgres, not column-scoped, and `hoods` already carries `001`'s one public-select policy; a new column is visible under an existing row policy automatically, there's nothing to add.
- **`USING (true)` on four policies, checked against what it actually exposes rather than accepted as a known-pattern label:** all four (`hoods`, `hood_density` pre-existing; `places`, `place_types` new) hold zero user identity, zero per-user rows, and zero write path for any client-held role (`anon`/`authenticated`) — confirmed by reading every column in both new tables (T-042 §3.2/§3.1: `id`, `name`, `category`, `place_type`, `hood_id`, `latitude`, `longitude`, `keywords`, `permanently_closed`, `closed_checked_at`, `is_tourist_trap`, `updated_at` — all curated-business reference data, none of it a user's location, visit, or timestamp; T-042 §3.4 states this explicitly and I checked it against the schema rather than taking the TRD's word for it). `using (true)` here means "public reference data, same response for every caller" by design, not "leak" — the distinction the checklist asks for. No table in either migration stores anything a restrictive policy would need to gate.
- **RLS logic holes (join to an open table, or a policy keying off a client-settable column):** checked specifically. `places.hood_id` FKs to `hoods.id`, and the fetch contract (T-042 §4.5) is PostgREST's embedded-resource syntax (`GET /rest/v1/hoods?select=id,blurb,places(...)`) — both sides of that join carry the identical `using (true)` policy, so there's no elevation: a caller who could already read all of `hoods` and all of `places` separately gets nothing new through the join. No policy in either migration reads a column the client can set (there is no write path at all, so this class of hole has no foothold here).
- **Storage buckets, rate limits, payments, AI/LLM, auth, SSRF:** none of these surfaces exist in either TRD — pure schema/RLS/reference-data work, no new endpoint, no external fetch, no secret. Confirmed `export_hoods_geojson.py` (the one script that does exist) reads `DATABASE_URL` from the environment only (`os.environ.get`, no hardcoded literal, no fallback default) — consistent with `database/README.md`'s "no secrets in SQL" rule, and the same convention both TRDs commit their still-unwritten scripts (`validate_dataset.py`, `build_hoods.py`, `export_places.py`) to follow.
- **`on delete restrict` (both new FKs into `places`, replacing an earlier `cascade` draft in T-033's superseded migration) is a genuine hardening, not a new surface** — it converts a silent data-loss path (a Hood geometry revision cascading away curated places) into a loud migration failure. Noted as a positive, not a finding.
- **Migration-number collision (`003`/`004`/`006`) re-checked independently rather than trusted from prior reviewers' say-so:** no collision exists as currently specified, and no stray file on disk contradicts it — `database/scripts/` holds only `export_hoods_geojson.py` today, no `003`/`004`/`006` file has been generated yet by either task.
- **Findings to relay:** none. No Critical/High/Medium/Low items to hand to `chief-of-staff` for a ticket — both TRDs are clean on every checklist item that applies to schema/RLS work, and the items that don't apply (storage, rate limits, payments, AI, auth, SSRF) aren't present in either surface.
- **Did not:** touch any migration file, edit either TRD, touch `BOARD.md` or Linear, or create any ticket (nothing to escalate).
- **Left behind:** nothing new. The standing recommendation this sweep was requested to close out (three prior worklog entries: `developer`, two `code-reviewer` signatures, `ios-developer`, all on T-033's `trd-review`) is now actioned — this is that sweep, and it found nothing blocking. Re-run this same sweep once `003`/`004`/`006` actually exist as generated files (post-`build`) to confirm the generated SQL matches what these TRDs specify — a TRD is not the artifact that gets applied.

### 2026-07-31 — architect — T-032/PAS-15: edge-gesture feasibility read (NOT a TRD) — both edges are buildable on iPhone; the left-edge back gesture is not the blocker, iPad and the sheet axis are

- **Scope:** narrow pre-design technical-feasibility read dispatched ahead of `designer`, on the founder-direct gesture model recorded in the FOUNDER-DIRECT STUB below ("both edges. its not swipe from left to right..you slide the you finder from up to down on one of the edges"). Recommendation only — no TRD written, no module boundaries or file layout chosen, `prds/time-slider/TRD.md` untouched.
- **Headline: the premise the dispatch was built on does not hold for this app.** iOS's interactive pop/back gesture is **not** an OS-level screen-edge gesture — it belongs to `UINavigationController`/`NavigationStack` and only exists while a stack has depth ≥ 2. Verified directly in `passenger-code/`: `grep` for `NavigationStack|NavigationView|UINavigationController|interactivePopGestureRecognizer` across every `.swift` file returns **zero hits**; `PassengerApp.swift` puts `MapScreen()` straight into `WindowGroup`. There is no back gesture on the map screen today, and none is reachable from it. Even after a future Profile tab / pushed detail lands, the map is the **root** of its stack, where the pop recognizer is inert by construction. Axis is a second, independent defence: `UIScreenEdgePanGestureRecognizer(.left)` is direction-constrained to rightward translation and fails on a vertical pan. **Verdict on the question as asked: coexistence is not the hard problem, and right-edge-only would buy nothing against it.**
- **Four constraints that are real, found by checking rather than assumed:**
  1. **iPad inverts the answer, and the app ships iPad.** `TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY = "1,2"` in `Passenger.xcodeproj/project.pbxproj` (6 occurrences, both targets). On iPadOS the **right** edge is the system Slide Over / multitasking reveal — a genuine OS gesture an app cannot disable. So the intuitive "right edge is safer" is backwards here: on iPad the *right* edge is the contested one and the left is clean. Any "either edge" spec needs a per-idiom answer.
  2. **Both edges are reserved at their top and bottom ends, on every device.** Bottom ~20-30pt is the home-indicator zone (swipe-up wins over the app); the top of the left edge is Notification Center and the top of the right edge is Control Center. `MapScreen` is `.ignoresSafeArea()`, so an edge strip inherits the full screen height unless deliberately inset. The usable track is therefore inset at **both** ends — which directly taxes req 1's new v2 bullet ("all 13 positions reachable in one vertical drag at max Dynamic Type"), since the vertical axis was already the shorter one.
  3. **A presented sheet's dismiss gesture is on the same axis as the slider.** `MapScreen.swift:216` already presents `HoodStubSheet` with `.presentationDetents([.medium])`, and T-033/T-038 add more. A vertical drag started on an edge over a presented sheet drags **the sheet**, not the slider — and the sheet's dismiss recognizer is not something an app-level gesture outranks. This collides head-on with req 2's "any open sheet is unchanged by an hour change," which reads as though the control should be usable with a sheet up. This is a bigger practical conflict than the back gesture ever was.
  4. **MapKit pan arbitration, which this repo has already been bitten by once.** `MapScreen.swift:57-66` carries a documented workaround (FB19394663) for MapKit swallowing gestures. An edge strip that reliably beats MapKit's pan must sit above the `Map` and consume touches inside it — permanently removing a band of map from panning near both edges. Not fatal; a real cost designers should be pricing in, not discovering at build.
- **Recommendation for `designer` and `product` to design around — plainly: keep both edges, do not fall back to right-edge-only.** Right-edge-only solves a problem this app does not have and creates one it does (iPad Slide Over). Concretely: (a) inset the activation strip vertically clear of the home-indicator and Notification/Control Center zones, and size the 13-stop track inside what survives; (b) require a small vertical-dominant initial displacement before the control claims the touch — cheap insurance that also helps against MapKit pan and against any future nav stack; (c) treat iPad as its own answer (left-edge-only, or gesture on iPhone only); (d) get a product answer on sheet-open behaviour — whether the gesture is simply unavailable while a sheet is up. **Do not reach for `preferredScreenEdgesDeferringSystemGestures`** — it defers rather than disables (users get a two-swipe home gesture), it is a `UIViewController` property with no SwiftUI equivalent in this app's structure, and it is an HIG/App-Store smell for a non-immersive map app.
- **Why the residual risk is low, and this is the load-bearing point for design:** Aviran resolved open question 1 to **supplement** — the heat-button/modal path stays. Every context where the gesture is genuinely unavailable (sheet presented, iPad right edge, VoiceOver/Switch Control per req 6) already has a working second path. None of the four constraints above is a launch blocker as long as the design does not assume the gesture is the *only* way in.
- **[ASSUMPTION] iOS 26 specifics.** Deployment target is `IPHONEOS_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET = 26.0` (both configs). My reading of the reserved-edge zones is the long-standing iOS/iPadOS behaviour; I did not verify against iOS 26's own release notes, and this codebase already documents one iOS 26 gesture regression (FB19394663). Whoever builds this should confirm the reserved-zone geometry on a real iOS 26 device rather than take these dimensions from me.
- **Did not:** write a TRD or any new document, edit `prds/time-slider/time-slider.md` or its `TRD.md`, edit `strategy/passenger-strategy.md`, touch `BOARD.md` or Linear, or change any code. Did not stage the 10 uncommitted `agents-mirror/*.md` or the 2 untracked `design/*.md` — still `T-045`'s, still nobody's, refused again rather than swept in.
- **Git:** committed to `passenger-brain` (branch `main`), explicit path only — `agent-os/PROGRESS.md`. **Committed, not pushed — `git remote -v` returns empty, verified this turn, not assumed** (L-015, `PAS-21`, still Aviran's).

### 2026-07-31 — developer — T-043 security fix: `revoke execute` added to §4.1's hood_for_point()/reattribute_events(), FK divergence and 2 verification notes made explicit in TRD text

- **Did:** fixed the HIGH-severity finding from `security-auditor`'s `trd-review` on `prds/live-events-pipeline/TRD.md` (T-043) — this is a text fix, not a migration, since no SQL file has been written for this task yet. §4.1's `hood_for_point()` and `reattribute_events()` had no `revoke execute` statement, the same bug class already fixed once on migration 002 (T-031): Postgres grants EXECUTE to PUBLIC on every new function, and Supabase auto-exposes it as a PostgREST RPC. `reattribute_events()` is the sharp edge — it runs a bulk `update` across `events` and, unrevoked, would be a callable `rpc/reattribute_events` on the public anon key, an unauthenticated write-amplification endpoint currently blunted only *implicitly* by `events`' own RLS (a coincidence, not a control). Added `revoke execute on function public.hood_for_point(double precision, double precision), public.reattribute_events(text) from public, anon, authenticated`, mirroring §4.3's existing pattern (same phrasing, same citation to migration 002's incident) — §4.3's ranking functions already had this; §4.1's two were simply missed. Also updated §9's A3 build step to call out the revoke explicitly, same treatment §9 already gives B4.
- **Also fixed, same pass (relayed mid-task, a second reviewer's finding on the same TRD):** §3.2's `events.hood_id ... on delete set null` silently contradicted `hood-dataset/TRD.md` (T-040 §8), which states `events.hood_id` should follow `places.hood_id`'s `restrict` rule. Judged on the merits, then confirmed against `code-reviewer`'s own read of the same question (relayed a second time, mid-fix): `set null` is the more correct choice here, not a defect. `places` needs `restrict` because a place silently losing its Hood is data loss on a hand-curated row; `events` are numerous, machine-ingested, ephemeral (90-day retention) and already re-attachable by design — `hood_id = null` is a normal ingest-time state, not a failure a constraint should guard. Concretely, `restrict` would **break T-040's own build step**: `hood-dataset/TRD.md` §3.3's scoped `delete from hoods` (placeholder rows dropped when the real dataset lands) would fail outright the moment any placeholder Hood had attributed events. Kept `set null`, now a stated decision in §3.2 (new second bullet) with that mechanism named explicitly, rather than a silent divergence from a sibling TRD.
- **Two lower-severity build-time verification notes from `security-auditor`, now explicit TRD requirements rather than private notes:** (1) §4.2 and §9 A2 now name all four base tables (`events`, `event_sources`, `event_source_links`, `event_ingest_runs`) explicitly and require `code-review`/`security-auditor` to confirm `pg_class.relrowsecurity` on all four individually before sign-off — not three-of-four by assumption. (2) §4.4 and §9 A4 now require confirming `anon`/`authenticated` hold no grant on `pg_net`'s own internal schema (`net.http_request_queue`, `net._http_response`) — those tables log the outbound request including the service-role Bearer token header used for the ingestion fetch, so an accessible read there would leak the same secret Vault exists to protect.
- **Two more minors, relayed from `code-reviewer`'s pass, same fix batch:** (1) every `create table`/`create index` in §3 (`event_sources`, `events` + its 3 indexes, `event_source_links` + its index, `event_ingest_runs`) lacked `if not exists`, unlike migrations `001`/`002`'s established idempotent convention — added throughout, plus a one-line note in §3's intro. (2) §4.2's `with (security_invoker = false)` requires Postgres 15+ and no TRD in this project had stated the project's actual Supabase Postgres version — added an explicit pre-A2 confirmation requirement plus a named fallback (a `security definer` wrapper function) if the project turns out to be older.
- **Did not:** write or touch any migration file — TRD is still pre-build, no SQL exists yet for T-043. Did not touch `BOARD.md` or Linear.
- **Left behind:** this closes the fix pass `chief-of-staff` dispatched (both findings named in the 2026-07-31 consolidation entry below). Migration file still needs to be written against this corrected TRD (`code-reviewer`/`security-auditor` may want to re-confirm the §4.1 wording lands unchanged in the actual SQL when A1/A3 are built). Commit `<see next git log entry>`.

### 2026-07-31 — developer — T-040 `trd-review`, backend track (A1, plus B6's SQL half): APPROVE the schema and upsert/prune design — one migration-numbering collision found, needs a TRD text fix before B6 is built

- **Did:** reviewed `prds/hood-dataset/TRD.md` (commit `2eac160`) §3.1 (schema, migration `003_hood_attributes.sql`), §3.3 (the generated data migration's upsert+prune), §4.4/D6 (the `places.hood_id` cascade→restrict ratification), and §8 D4/D6 against migration `001`'s actual committed SQL and `database/README.md`'s numbering rule. Confirmed the four things the dispatch asked for by reading the real `001_hoods_and_density.sql` on disk, not the TRD's paraphrase of it.
- **Schema (A1) — correct as specified, no changes needed.** `blurb text` nullable (null = not curated, `""` never stored, rejected at authoring time by V8); `is_tourist_trap boolean` nullable, genuinely three states (`null`/`false`/`true`) because `tourist-trap-flag` reqs 4 and 7 both need the null-vs-false distinction preserved through to VoiceOver — a `not null default false` here would collapse it and make req 7 unimplementable, matching this task's own prohibition list; `designated_for_progression boolean not null default false`, correctly the opposite shape because `passport` req 4 has no unknown state and every existing row needs to be correct with no backfill. All three are `add column if not exists`, idempotent, no RLS change needed — new columns inherit `001`'s existing row-level `select` policy (RLS is row-scoped, not column-scoped, so this claim is literally true, not just usually true). No write policy anywhere, consistent with the standing pattern.
- **Upsert + city-scoped prune (§3.3) — confirmed this actually closes the gap, not just plausible on its face.** Read `001` directly: A3 does write `on conflict (id) do nothing`, and its own header comment claims the real export "supersedes these rows by id (upsert-shaped)" — comment and SQL genuinely disagree, exactly as the TRD states. Traced both failure paths the new design has to close: (1) **shared ids** (`florentin`, `neve-tzedek`, `lev-hair`, possibly others) — `on conflict (id) do update set` overwrites every mutable column including `polygon`, so the placeholder rectangle is actually replaced, not left in place; (2) **dropped ids** (a placeholder Hood the real dataset doesn't reuse) — the `delete ... where city = 'tel-aviv' and id <> all(array[...])` scoped-prune removes exactly those rows and no others. Both paths are genuinely idempotent (re-running the same generated file twice converges to the same end state), which satisfies this project's additive-idempotent migration convention even though this file is a `delete`, not just an `add column`. `city`-scoping correctly protects a future second city from a Tel-Aviv-only prune. **Gap closed, not just addressed on paper.**
- **D6/`on delete restrict` — ratified from the hoods side, nothing here depends on cascade.** Checked whether this migration's own design needs cascade-deleting any dependent of `hoods`: it doesn't. The only cascade this task's own prune relies on is `hood_density.hood_id ... on delete cascade` (`001`, unaffected by this TRD) — correct, because that data is hourly-regenerated and disposable, unlike curated places. If `places.hood_id` were cascade instead of restrict, this task's own prune-delete (§3.3) would silently delete curated places the moment a geometry revision drops a Hood id — the exact hazard D6 exists to prevent, and the exact reason the prune has to `restrict` rather than `cascade` to be safe. Agree with T-042's ratification; `restrict` is clean here, no design in this task pulls the other way.
- **Finding (not previously flagged on this task) — the TRD's own migration-number example collides with the now-resolved cross-task numbering.** §3.3 line ~184 and §4.5's CLI contract both illustrate `build_hoods.py --migration-number 004` → `004_hoods_tel_aviv_data.sql`. But this file's own PROGRESS.md entries above (T-042 `trd-review`, both signatures) record the numbering as **resolved workspace-wide: `003` = hood-dataset, `004` = places-dataset, `005` = live-events-pipeline** — one number per *task*. T-040 structurally needs **two** migration files, not one: `003_hood_attributes.sql` (schema, A1, hand-written) and a second, generated data migration (§3.3, B6) that doesn't exist yet. The TRD's own worked example for that second file reuses `004` — already spoken for by T-042's `004_places.sql`. This isn't cosmetic: `database/README.md`'s own rule is "sequential, never renumbered," and two files claiming the same number is exactly the race the TRD itself warns about one paragraph earlier ("three TRDs are in flight against this same directory and a race there produces two files with the same number and no error," §3.3). Needs a fix before B6 runs: either the TRD's example is restated with a placeholder rather than a literal stale number, or a fourth slot (e.g. `006`, after all three tasks' primary migrations) is explicitly reserved for T-040's data migration and recorded in `database/README.md` when B6 lands. Not a schema defect — a sequencing correction `architect` or `chief-of-staff` needs to make before `developer` runs `build_hoods.py` for real.
- **Minor, non-blocking:** the generated file (§3.3's shape) isn't shown wrapped in an explicit transaction. The insert/upsert and the delete are each independently idempotent, so a partial apply (e.g., a paste interrupted between the two statements) can't corrupt state into something silently wrong — worst case is a stale dropped-id row surviving until the next full apply, which is a mild version of the exact bug this task fixes, not a new one. Worth a `begin;`/`commit;` wrap for cleanliness when `build_hoods.py` is actually written, not blocking `trd-review`.
- **Verdict: APPROVE A1's schema and §3.3's upsert+prune design as correct and gap-closing. One finding needs resolution before B6 is built** (migration-numbering collision, above) — narrow, a TRD-text/sequencing fix, not a redesign. D6's `restrict` ratified from the hoods side with no reservation.

### 2026-07-31 — code-reviewer — T-043 `trd-review`, second signature (A1-A4 + B1-B7): REQUEST CHANGES, independently corroborates `developer`'s two blocking findings, adds 2 new minors

- **Did:** reviewed `prds/live-events-pipeline/TRD.md` (commit `e142e91`) cold — read the TRD in full, then migrations `001`/`002` and `database/README.md` line by line to check the RLS/revoke idiom against the actual established pattern (not the TRD's description of it), then `hood-dataset/TRD.md` and `places-dataset/TRD.md` directly for the cross-task ray-cast question — **before** reading `developer`'s and `data-engineer`'s entries below, specifically so my read would be independent corroboration rather than a re-statement of theirs. Compared after the fact.
- **RLS/revoke security pass (the mandated primary pass on this migration) — the core design holds up under adversarial reasoning, with one real gap.** Traced the full access path by hand: RLS enabled + zero policies on all four base tables is default-deny for every role except owner/`bypassrls`, independent of any grant; `revoke all ... from anon, authenticated` is a second, independent control on top of that (removes the table-level grant itself), so a mistake in either layer alone (RLS not enabled, or the revoke omitted) is still caught by the other — correctly redundant, not just decorative. `events_public`'s `security_invoker = false` is the right mechanism for the view to read through the revoked/RLS-denied base tables (it executes as the view owner, who — as owner, with no `force row level security` set on any base table — bypasses RLS by default): this is the standard, legitimate Postgres pattern for a security-definer view as sole read path, not a workaround. Column projection correctly drops `dedup_key`, `primary_source`, `ingested_at`, `end_at_estimated`. **The one real gap, independently reached, matches `developer`'s finding 1 exactly:** `hood_for_point()` and `reattribute_events()` (§4.1) have no `revoke execute` and no stated security mode (definer vs. invoker), unlike every other function in this document (§4.3's three ranking functions all get `revoke execute ... from public, anon, authenticated`, citing migration `002`'s HIGH finding by name). `reattribute_events()` is write-capable — it can re-run attribution across every row in `events` — so this is the identical exploit shape as `002`'s HIGH finding if the function ever ships (or is later changed to) `security definer`: an anon-key holder calling `POST /rest/v1/rpc/reattribute_events` repeatedly gets unbounded, unauthenticated write-amplification with no auth check possible, because nothing in this text rules that mode out. Confirmed by direct grep of §4.1 and §9 A3 — no revoke anywhere in either. **Concur with `developer`: blocking, needs the same revoke + an explicit security-mode statement added to A3 before build.**
- **Cross-TRD `hood_for_point()` consistency (the third instructed check) — confirmed inconsistent, not resolvable inside this TRD alone.** Read `hood-dataset/TRD.md` and `places-dataset/TRD.md`'s own text directly rather than trusting either summary: both state, in near-identical language, that the containment/ray-cast check is enforced by `database/scripts/validate_dataset.py` — offline stdlib Python, run at authoring time over hand-authored files, **explicitly not Postgres** ("There is no PostGIS on this project... a DB-level containment constraint would mean adding a spatial extension for one authoring-time check"). T-043 §4.1/§8 F7 claims `hood_for_point()` is "the same primitive `places-dataset` req 1 needs... whichever of T-042 and T-043 builds first owns the function; the other consumes it" — that framing cannot be literally true, since T-042 never calls a Postgres function for this at all. Net: two independent, necessary implementations of the identical even-odd ray-cast (Python at authoring time, SQL at ingest time) with no shared test vectors and no stated on-boundary convention for `hood_for_point()` (T-040's Python side pins on-boundary to `false` explicitly; T-043 lists on-boundary as a unit-test case in A3 without stating the expected result). Failure scenario: a place and a live event at the same coordinate on a shared Hood edge could silently resolve to different Hoods, with nothing in either test suite positioned to catch it. **This is not a new finding — `developer`'s entry below, `data-engineer`'s entry below, and my own earlier T-042 `trd-review` pass (commit `78f24a9`, further below) already reached the same conclusion independently — but three-for-three convergence from three separate reviewers is worth stating plainly as settled, not still-open-to-debate.** Routing stays `chief-of-staff`/`architect`'s: either correct §4.1/F7's wording to describe a documented cross-language conformance check (one checked-in fixture of point→expected-hood_id cases, including on-boundary, run against both implementations) or genuinely unify the two — not mine to pick.
- **`events.hood_id ... on delete set null` (§3.2) vs. `hood-dataset/TRD.md`'s explicit "should follow the same `restrict` rule" (§8 risk table) — confirmed a real, undocumented divergence, matching `developer`'s finding 2.** Formed my own view on the merits before reading `developer`'s take: I read `set null` as very likely the *more* correct choice for `events` specifically, not just an oversight — events are machine-ingested, numerous, and already designed to tolerate `hood_id = null` as an ordinary state (§3.2's own F1 discussion, `reattribute_events()` is the designed repair path), whereas `places` are curated, few, and expensive, which is exactly why `restrict` is right there. If `events.hood_id` also used `restrict`, T-040's own Hood-prune step (`delete from hoods where city = 'tel-aviv' and id not in (...)`) would fail outright the moment any live event referenced a dropped Hood id — plausible on nearly every geometry revision, since events churn constantly. That reasoning is nowhere in T-043's text, though, and T-040's audit line reads as a settled expectation this TRD silently contradicts. Concur with `developer`: needs one sentence in §3.2 stating the rationale, and T-040's audit line corrected to match rather than left claiming an FK behavior this TRD doesn't implement.
- **Two new, additive minors, not yet flagged by `developer` or `data-engineer`'s passes:** (1) **Migration-safety/idempotency.** Every `create table` shown in §3.1-3.4 (`event_sources`, `events`, `event_source_links`, `event_ingest_runs`) and their indexes are plain `create table`/`create index`, no `if not exists` guard — migrations `001`/`002` and `places-dataset/TRD.md`'s shown DDL all use `if not exists`/`create or replace`/`on conflict`, and `database/README.md`'s own convention plus this review's mandated migration-safety pass both call for exactly this. A paste-twice re-run of this migration as currently shown would error on the second run. Likely a TRD-illustrative-SQL omission, not a deliberate choice, but worth naming before it reaches the real file. (2) **`with (security_invoker = false)` needs Postgres 15+.** The view's security-definer behavior is correct by default on any Postgres version (pre-15 views always ran this way), but the explicit reloption syntax itself only exists from PG15 onward — `developer`/`ios-developer` should confirm the Supabase project's Postgres version before A2, or drop the explicit clause (equivalent to omitting it pre-15).
